c.tagline: Oil-boom capital on Bioko Island where colonial Spain meets equatorial jungle.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are not used; shared taxis run fixed low-cost routes while private rides are negotiated with the driver before departure, typically in XAF cash.

emergency.note: Fire: 112. Traffic police: 116. Numbers are inconsistently answered; contact your hotel or embassy for assistance, and expats typically rely on private clinics.

hood_landmark.Sipopo: Sofitel Malabo Sipopo Le Golf, Sipopo

hood_desc: Colonial downtown centered on Plaza de la Independencia and the Catedral de Santa Isabel, with government buildings, banks and the city's best restaurants within walking distance; suits business travelers and first-time visitors wanting to be central.
The city's authentic working-class barrio south of downtown, with its bustling open-air market and low-rise Spanish-colonial-era housing; suits budget travelers wanting a local, non-touristy base.

The corridor along the airport road roughly 3km from downtown, home to business hotels used by oil-industry visitors; suits travelers with early flights or business meetings who want easy airport access.

A purpose-built resort and diplomatic enclave east of the city, created for the 2011/2012 African Union summits, with golf, beach access and embassies; suits luxury travelers and conference attendees wanting resort isolation.
A beachfront barrio north of the center known for its black volcanic sand shoreline and seafood stalls; suits visitors who want a coastal feel while staying close to the city.

water.note: Tap water is unsafe for visitors; stick to bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash (XAF) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no electronic ticketing system. Shared taxis charge a small fixed per-seat fare along fixed routes, while private taxi rides are negotiated before departure since meters are not used.
transit.hours: Daytime only, roughly 6am-9pm; there is little to no public transit after dark and visitors rely on hotel cars or pre-arranged drivers at night.
transit.note: Public transport is limited and infrequent; most visitors and expats rely on private cars, hotel shuttles, or negotiated taxis rather than buses.

bus: Malabo Urban Bus (limited routes, e.g. Centro-Ela Nguema)
ferry: Ferries to Bata and Douala, Cameroon from Malabo Port

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected, though rounding up or leaving small change at upscale hotels and restaurants catering to expats is appreciated.
